claims.text: In 1906 the Ottoman Empire and the British Empire fixed the border between the region and Egypt; Britain occupied the territory in 1917–18 and ruled it from 1920 to 1948 as part of Mandatory Palestine.

Gaza had a pre-war population of about 40,000; British and Commonwealth forces were defeated at the First and Second Battles of Gaza in March and April 1917; the Third Battle was fought on the night of 1–2 November 1917; Ottoman forces evacuated the town on the night of 6–7 November and the EEF occupied it on 7 November; the bombardment severely damaged or destroyed the majority of the city's housing.

Village Statistics, 1945: Gaza Subdistrict 137,180 people (133,040 Muslims, 2,890 Jews, 1,250 Christians); Gaza town 34,250 (33,160 Muslims, 80 Jews, 1,010 Christians); all localities captured by Israel were depopulated before, during or after the 1948 war (al-Majdal was not destroyed); Egypt held the southern and central parts, which became the Gaza Strip.

Gaza's Jewish community, renewed in the late 19th century mainly by Sephardi traders, had close to a hundred members before World War I, was largely expelled by the Ottomans during the war, numbered 51 in 1926, and ended in the 1929 riots, when its members left by train for Lod with help from some local Arabs and British police.

Kfar Darom was founded on 6 October 1946 on the site of an orchard established in 1930; Egyptian regular forces attacked it on 15 May 1948 and were repelled; it was evacuated on the night of 8 July 1948; after 1967 a Nahal settlement was built nearby in 1970, civilianized in 1989, and evacuated on 18 August 2005.
Kfar Darom, a small kibbutz that existed for about 18 months between 1946 and 1948, was part of the Jewish Agency's '11 points in the Negev' plan.
Morris describes Majdal as lying next to the site of the Philistine port of Ashkelon.

entries.topic: The 1948 war in the south and the making of the strip

claims.text: Operation Yoav (15 October–4 November 1948) aimed to link Israeli forces in the Negev with those to the north; Israeli artillery and air power were used to soften villages before occupation; by its end Israeli forces had defeated the Egyptian army on the southern front and occupied most villages of the Gaza District (citing Morris).

Before 1948 Gaza was one of Mandate Palestine's districts, comprising the Gaza and Bir al-Sabi' subdistricts; Israel took all of Bir al-Sabi' and most of the Gaza subdistrict in 1948; the remainder became the Gaza Strip, 361 square kilometres, about 1.3 percent of Palestine.

Golan (2024) gives the strip's area as 365 square kilometres and traces its formation from UNSCOP's September 1947 allocation of the southern coastal strip to a prospective Arab state to the February 1950 Modus Vivendi, describing it as an allegedly provisional entity of undetermined formal status.

The Modus Vivendi signed at El Auja on 22 February 1950 set patrol zones in the Gaza–Rafah area 'of a purely local character' and stated that it did not change either party's position on the armistice demarcation line.
The 1949 armistice line separated Egyptian and Israeli forces and became the Gaza–Israel boundary; both signatories declared it was not an international border.

Al-Majdal had about 10,000 residents before the war; it was captured on 4 November 1948 with about 1,000 Arabs remaining, about 2,700 by 1950; in June 1950 the government began moving them out, many to Gaza, with Ben-Gurion's authorization and at Moshe Dayan's urging; Ben-Gurion suspended the operation in October 1950 after Histadrut objections (Stein, summarizing Morris).
Tens of thousands of Palestinian refugees fled or were expelled to the Gaza Strip in 1948 (citing Farrell, Reuters, 2023).
The principal Egyptian–Israeli General Armistice Agreement was signed at Rhodes on 24 February 1949.

Article VI(1) of the Egyptian–Israeli armistice set the Gaza–Rafah demarcation line 'as delineated in paragraph 2.B (i) of the Memorandum of 13 November 1948', from the coast at the mouth of Wadi Hasi east through Deir Suneid, across the Gaza–al-Majdal highway and south parallel to it to the Egyptian frontier; Article VI(2) held Egyptian forces to their positions and required Israeli forces to withdraw from Beit Hanun and its area to north of the line.

claims.text: The strip's initial post-war population was about 80,000, and refugees from the rest of the Gaza subdistrict and the Lydda district exceeded 200,000; they were first housed in mosques, schools, homes, barracks and open ground; the American Friends Service Committee set up camps on land allocated by Egypt; the encyclopedia lists Jabaliya and Nussayrat (1948), al-Maghazi, Deir al-Balah, Khan Yunis and Rafah (1949), Shati' (1951) and al-Bureij (1952); UNRWA, founded on 8 December 1949, began operating on 1 May 1950.
By the war's end a quarter of Mandatory Palestine's Arab population was in Gaza, on about 1 percent of the land (Filiu); more than 200,000 refugees came into Gaza (Efrat; Baster).

Resolution 302 (IV) of 8 December 1949 established UNRWA to carry out direct relief and works programmes, recognized that continued assistance was necessary 'to prevent conditions of starvation', and set 1 April 1950 for taking over from the earlier UN relief body.

Egypt administered the strip through a military governor and never annexed it; it did not give Gaza's Palestinians citizenship and issued All-Palestine travel documents; it restricted movement in and out of Gaza; the All-Palestine Government moved to Cairo and was dissolved by Nasser in 1959.

The Basic Law of the Gaza Strip was issued in 1955 and entered into force in 1958, reserving four Legislative Council seats for refugees; Egypt issued identity documents to refugees and non-refugees alike.
AFP, citing UNRWA, reported in November 2023 that more than two-thirds of Gaza's 2.4 million residents were registered refugees, in eight camps set up after the 1948 exodus.

Per Morris (summarized by Stein), the Majdal transfer began on 14 June 1950 and Ben-Gurion authorized it on 19 June on condition the residents agreed; Morris attributes the departures mainly to systematic intimidation; residents signed forms declaring their departure voluntary; most went to Gaza, some to Lod and Ramle.
In 1961 Egypt issued new travel documents for Gaza's residents without the All-Palestine Government's name.
The area was controlled by the Ottoman Empire from the 16th century.
